title: UML Class Diagrams
intro: How to read and draw UML class diagrams: the class box, visibility, the six relationship lines, multiplicity, object diagrams and stereotypes, and how each symbol turns into Java code (and back).

cards.title: UML and the class box
cards.body:
**UML** (Unified Modeling Language) is a *visual* language for specifying, documenting and communicating software designs (Booch, Jacobson & Rumbaugh, 1996; adopted by OMG). It has **structure** diagrams (class, object, package...) and **behaviour** diagrams (use case, activity, sequence...).
A **class diagram** shows classes and the relationships between them. Each class is a box with 3 compartments.

cards.title: Attribute and operation syntax
cards.body:
Attributes: `visibility name : Type [multiplicity] = initial-value`
Operations: `visibility name(param : Type, ...) : ReturnType`
Note the order is **name first, type second**, the opposite of Java. Parts can be omitted in a rough sketch (e.g. just `close()`).

Return type goes AFTER the brackets: `+ getName() : String`
`void` methods may show `: void` or nothing

cards.title: Visibility symbols
cards.body: Every attribute and operation starts with a visibility symbol. There are four, matching Java's four access levels. The one people mix up: **# is protected**, **~ is package** (Java's default, written with *no* keyword).

cards.title: Static, abstract, interface, constant
cards.body:
Three styles change the meaning of a name:
**Underline** = static (belongs to the class, one shared copy).
**Italics** or `{abstract}` = abstract class / abstract method.
`<<interface>>` written above the name = an interface.
A constant (`public static final`) is underlined (static), usually in CAPS; standard UML adds `{readOnly}` for final (slides just show CAPS).

cards.title: Association: navigability and role names
cards.body:
An **association** (solid line) means objects of one class hold a long-lived reference to objects of the other, i.e. a **field**.
**Navigability**: an open arrowhead means 'can navigate this way'. With an arrow from A to B, only A gets a field. With no arrowheads it is bi-directional and **both** classes get a field.
The **role name** at an end becomes the field name in the class at the *other* end.

cards.title: Aggregation vs composition
cards.body:
Both are **whole-part** ('has a') associations, and the diamond is **always at the whole**.
**Aggregation** (hollow): parts are standalone; they exist independently and may be shared.
**Composition** (filled): the whole creates and owns its parts; a part belongs to at most one whole, and dies with it.

cards.title: Generalisation vs realisation
cards.body:
**Generalisation** = inheritance ('is a'): solid line, hollow triangle pointing at the **superclass**. Java `extends`.
**Realisation** = a class implements an interface: **dashed** line, hollow triangle pointing at the **interface**. Java `implements`.
An interface that extends another interface is generalisation, so the line is **solid**.

cards.title: Object diagrams
cards.body: An **object diagram** is a snapshot of actual objects at one moment. Each box is labelled `objectName : ClassName`, **underlined**. The attribute compartment shows **values** (`name = "Jack"`), not types. Lines between objects are **links** (instances of an association) and carry no multiplicity. An unnamed object is written `:Book` (anonymous object); a state can be shown in brackets, e.g. `[checked out]`.

cards.title: Stereotypes
cards.body:
A **stereotype** is a label in guillemets `<< >>` that gives an element an extra meaning. The slides classify classes by responsibility:
**<<entity>>** persistent information the system tracks (Student, Course).
**<<boundary>>** interaction with the outside (InvoiceForm, xxxUI).
**<<control>>** logic that coordinates a use case (CourseMgr, xxxCtrl).
